title: Tangible superiority before attacking

D0.outcome: Explains that an attack needs a tangible superiority at the point of attack (in working force or reach), and that without it the counter-attack finds the attacker disordered.

D1.outcome: In a middlegame position, counts the attacking pieces that bear on the target area against the defenders and says 'attack now', 'not yet' or 'no'.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses among attacking, finishing development and defending, and punishes a premature attack by the opponent.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a one-feature change (the opponent has castled and developed; the centre is closed) removes the licence to attack, and why a development deficit voids a tempting sacrifice.

D4.outcome: In own games, records the superiority count before attacking decisions, and the review compares it with the result.

misconceptions: Whoever has the initiative should attack.
Attack because it is my move.
An exposed king always justifies a sacrifice.
conditions: Attack when better developed, with more force aimed at the weak area and a concrete target.
A development lead licenses direct attack and can justify sacrifices to open lines; a development deficit voids it.
A very good opponent rarely offers the conditions for a quick attack.
contrasts: An attack on a fully developed opponent with no weak target (a premature attack that runs out of steam).
The same sacrifice when the opponent has castled and developed.
A closed centre or a quiet endgame-like position.
